label: Hirnantian glaciation
detail: The Late Ordovician icehouse, the first major glaciation of the Phanerozoic and one of the coldest intervals in the PhanDA 485-million-year reconstruction. It was short lived by deep-time standards and coincided with the end-Ordovician mass extinction.
uncertainty: stage boundaries about +/- 1 Myr

label: End-Permian hothouse
detail: The Permian-Triassic boundary, the largest extinction event of the Phanerozoic, accompanied by extreme global warmth in the PhanDA reconstruction. Siberian Traps volcanism is the usual proposed driver.
uncertainty: about +/- 0.1 Myr

label: Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
detail: The Chicxulub impact and the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. It is the zero point of the CENOGRID record, which begins at 66 Ma and runs continuously to the present.
uncertainty: about +/- 0.05 Myr

label: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
detail: A carbon release of 3,000 to more than 13,000 Pg C warmed the planet by 5 to 8 C, acidified the ocean and drove deep-sea extinction. The carbon-isotope excursion exceeded 2 per mil, with a body phase of 100 to 170 kyr and a recovery of 50 to 135 kyr, roughly 200 kyr in total. It is the closest deep-time analogue to the present, though almost certainly at a far slower release rate.
uncertainty: onset duration disputed, from about 1 kyr to more than 10 kyr

label: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
detail: The warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic and the CENOGRID Hothouse state. Poles were ice free, the equator-to-pole temperature gradient was shallow, and CO2 was far above present levels.
uncertainty: interval about 53.3-49.1 Ma

label: Eocene-Oligocene transition
detail: The abrupt step from a largely ice-free world to a glaciated Antarctica, visible as a sharp positive shift in benthic oxygen isotopes known as Oi-1. It marks the CENOGRID Warmhouse to Coolhouse boundary.
uncertainty: about +/- 0.1 Myr

label: Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum
detail: The last sustained interval substantially warmer than today, with partial retreat of the Antarctic ice sheet. It was followed by renewed cooling and ice growth through the late Miocene.
uncertainty: interval about 16.9-14.7 Ma

label: Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period
detail: The most recent multi-million-year interval warmer than the present, with CO2 broadly comparable to today. Benthic oxygen isotopes in the CENOGRID and LR04 records stay persistently lighter than Holocene values. It is the standard deep-time analogue for a stabilised warm world.
uncertainty: interval about 3.3-3.0 Ma

label: Northern Hemisphere glaciation begins
detail: The LR04 benthic stack shows a stepwise increase in mean oxygen-isotope values and in cycle amplitude as large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets become a persistent feature. From here on, glacial cycles are paced at roughly 41,000 years.
uncertainty: onset spread over about 3.0-2.5 Ma

label: Mid-Pleistocene Transition
detail: Glacial pacing shifts from about 41,000 to about 100,000 years, with larger, longer and more intense glaciations. No corresponding change occurs in the orbital forcing, so the cause must be internal to the climate system. Candidates include removal of subglacial regolith, deep-ocean cooling activating a sea-ice switch, a secular CO2 decline, and Antarctic ice reaching a critical size. It remains unresolved.
uncertainty: interval about 1.25-0.70 Ma

label: MIS 11 long interglacial
detail: An unusually long and warm interglacial, often invoked as an orbital analogue for the Holocene because eccentricity was similarly low. It is clearly resolved in the Antarctic 800,000-year composite CO2 record.
uncertainty: interval about 424-374 ka

label: Termination II
detail: The deglaciation from MIS 6 into the Last Interglacial, one of the great glacial terminations. Northern Africa and the Levant went through extreme aridity during the transition, and deep-water production was reduced before the interglacial stabilised.
uncertainty: about +/- 3 kyr; deglacial forcing usually modelled over 134-129 ka

label: Last Interglacial peak
detail: The Eemian, or MIS 5e. Sea level stood 6 to 9 m above present while CO2 was only 265 to 285 ppm, comparable to preindustrial, and global temperature was similar to or about 1 C above preindustrial. The warmth was driven by orbital forcing amplified by sea-ice, land-ice and vegetation feedbacks rather than by CO2, which makes it the best natural test of ice-sheet sensitivity to a small warming.
uncertainty: interval 129-116 ka; the highstand resolves into several sub-intervals

label: Last Glacial Maximum
detail: Nearly all ice sheets stood at their maximum positions from 26,500 to 19,000-20,000 years ago, after growing from 33,000 years ago as northern summer insolation, tropical Pacific sea surface temperature and CO2 all fell. Estimates of global cooling range from -4.5 to -7.0 C depending on the method used. Deglaciation began in the north at 19,000 to 20,000 years ago.
uncertainty: maximum ice extent 26,500-19,000 yr BP; a synchronous global LGM is itself debated

label: Termination I begins
detail: The onset of the last deglaciation, triggered by rising northern summer insolation, which released the abrupt sea-level rise that followed. The transition from here to the early Holocene is the largest climate change directly recorded by the ice cores.
uncertainty: onset 19,000-20,000 yr BP

label: Heinrich Stadial 1
detail: A prolonged North Atlantic cold stadial accompanying massive iceberg discharge from the Laurentide ice sheet. The Atlantic overturning circulation weakened and tropical rain belts shifted south.
uncertainty: interval about 17.5-14.7 ka

label: Meltwater Pulse 1A
detail: The most rapid sea-level rise of the last deglaciation: 14 to 18 m, with a full range of 12 to 22 m, in about 340 years. It was dated from drowned Tahitian corals recovered by IODP Expedition 310. Source attribution between the Laurentide, Eurasian and West Antarctic ice sheets is still open.
uncertainty: 14.65-14.31 ka; magnitude 14-18 m most probable

label: Bolling-Allerod warming
detail: The first abrupt Northern Hemisphere warming of the deglaciation, Greenland Interstadial 1e, of order 10 C over decades in Greenland. Antarctica cooled at the same time, the Antarctic Cold Reversal, in the classic expression of the bipolar seesaw.
uncertainty: GICC05 age 14,692 b2k; maximum counting error of order several hundred years at this depth

label: Antarctic Cold Reversal
detail: Antarctic cooling while the North Atlantic was warm, the southern half of the bipolar seesaw during the Bolling-Allerod. It is recorded in Antarctic ice-core deuterium.
uncertainty: interval about 14.7-13.0 ka

label: Younger Dryas begins
detail: Greenland Stadial 1: an abrupt return to near-glacial conditions in the North Atlantic region lasting about 1,200 years. It is usually attributed to a freshwater-driven weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation. The boundaries are formally defined in the INTIMATE event stratigraphy.
uncertainty: GICC05 age 12,896 b2k; quoted absolute error 100-140 years, though speleothem comparison suggests +/- 20-40 years

label: Younger Dryas ends, Holocene begins
detail: The termination of Greenland Stadial 1, defined from deuterium excess in the Greenland cores, with warming of several degrees within decades. This transition is also the global stratotype for the base of the Holocene and of the Greenlandian Age, fixed by convention at 11,700 years before 2000 CE.
uncertainty: GICC05 age 11,703 b2k, +/- 99 years maximum counting error; the GSSP is fixed at 11,700 b2k

label: 8.2 ka event
detail: The largest abrupt cooling of the Holocene, several degrees in Greenland and detectable across the Northern Hemisphere, attributed to the final drainage of glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway into the North Atlantic. Thomas and colleagues place the event between 8,297 and 8,136 years before 2000 CE, a duration of about 160 years. The stratotype for the Northgrippian Age sits inside it at 8,236 b2k.
uncertainty: GSSP fixed at 8,236 b2k; DYE-3 maximum counting error 47 years

label: Holocene Thermal Maximum
detail: Kaufman and colleagues place the warmest 200-year interval of the Holocene around 6,500 years ago, at 0.7 C above the 19th century with a 5th to 95th percentile range of 0.3 to 1.8 C, followed by cooling of 0.08 C per thousand years. This is contested: the Osman 2021 data assimilation finds no mid-Holocene maximum at all, and others argue the proxies record summer rather than annual temperature.
uncertainty: warmest 200-year interval about 6,500 yr BP; the existence of a global thermal maximum is disputed

label: 4.2 ka event
detail: An abrupt aridification recognised across the mid and low latitudes, marked by a shift to heavier oxygen isotopes in the Mawmluh Cave speleothem of Meghalaya, northeast India. That shift is the global stratotype for the base of the Meghalayan Age, ratified by the IUGS on 14 June 2018 and fixed at 4,250 years before 2000 CE, and corroborated by a cooling signal in the Mount Logan ice core. It is associated with the disruption of several Bronze Age societies.
uncertainty: GSSP fixed at 4,250 b2k; the monsoon weakening at the type section is dated 4,071-3,888 yr BP

label: Unidentified tropical eruption of 426 BCE
detail: The second largest volcanic stratospheric sulfur injection of the last 2,500 years in the eVolv2k version 4 ice-core catalogue. The source volcano has never been identified.
uncertainty: ice-core dated to within a few years; source unknown

label: Okmok II eruption, Alaska
detail: The third largest sulfur injection in the eVolv2k catalogue, tied to Okmok caldera in the Aleutians by tephra geochemistry. It coincides with the documented cold and famine of the closing years of the Roman Republic.
uncertainty: ice-core and tephra dated to 43 BCE

label: Roman Warm Period
detail: A conventionally named warm interval, roughly 250 BCE to 400 CE, well expressed in European and Mediterranean proxies. Global reconstructions of the past 2,000 years find no globally coherent warm epoch at this time, and the spatial coherence that exists is consistent with stochastic variability. Treat it as a regional label, not a global event.
uncertainty: no agreed boundaries; not globally coherent

label: The 536 CE dust veil
detail: Ice cores record sulfate peaks from eruptions in 536 and 540 CE plus a smaller event in 547. Tree rings from the Russian Altai and the European Alps show an unprecedented, spatially synchronised cooling, with decadal Northern Hemisphere volcanic forcing larger than any other period of the past 2,000 years and modelled peak anomalies beyond -2 C. Buntgen and colleagues named the following period the Late Antique Little Ice Age, 536 to about 660 CE. The source of the 536 event is undetermined, with Iceland a leading candidate.
uncertainty: eruption years ice-core dated to about +/- 1-2 years; the centennial duration of the cold period is debated

label: Medieval Climate Anomaly
detail: A conventionally named warm interval, roughly 950 to 1250 CE, prominent in North Atlantic and European records. As with the Roman Warm Period, global syntheses find no globally synchronous warm epoch, and IPCC AR6 avoids the term in favour of explicit dates.
uncertainty: no agreed boundaries; regionally asynchronous

label: Samalas eruption, Lombok
detail: The largest stratospheric sulfur release of the Common Era and of the past 7,000 years: at least 40 cubic kilometres of tephra as dense rock equivalent, an eruption column to 43 km and a magnitude of 7. Later measurements give 158 plus or minus 12 Tg of SO2 and 227 plus or minus 18 Tg of chlorine. Model simulations give a surface cooling of order 1 C, consistent with tree-ring reconstructions. The source was only identified in 2013, from tephra geochemistry matching shards in both Arctic and Antarctic ice.
uncertainty: eruption 1257 CE; the ice-core sulfate peak appears at 1258/1259 because of the deposition lag

label: Little Ice Age
detail: A multi-century cold interval, conventionally about 1300 to 1850 CE, driven by clustered volcanism and low solar activity and amplified by sea-ice and ocean feedbacks. It was not globally synchronous: the coldest century was the 15th in the central and eastern Pacific, the 17th in northwestern Europe and southeastern North America, and the mid-19th over most of the rest. IPCC AR6 dates its cessation to the late 1700s to mid 1800s.
uncertainty: boundaries are definitional rather than measured; regional coldest decades differ by up to 400 years

label: Sporer Minimum
detail: A roughly 90-year interval of very low solar activity, identified by John Eddy in 1976 from carbon-14 in tree rings rather than from sunspot counts, since it predates telescopic observation. It is named for the German astronomer Gustav Sporer.
uncertainty: about 1460-1550; inferred from carbon-14, not direct observation

label: Huaynaputina eruption, Peru
detail: One of the largest historical eruptions of South America and a major sulfur injection in the ice-core catalogue. It was followed by widely reported cold and famine across the Northern Hemisphere.
uncertainty: eruption 19 February 1600; ice-core sulfate dated to within a year or two

label: Maunder Minimum
detail: The deepest grand solar minimum of the observational era, with sunspots almost entirely absent for about 70 years and a solar wind perhaps half its modern speed. Reassessment of multiple datasets confirms activity well below the Dalton Minimum or recent cycles. It overlaps but does not explain the Little Ice Age, which began well before it.

label: Laki fissure eruption, Iceland
detail: An eight-month high-latitude fissure eruption that produced a persistent sulfurous haze over Europe, a severe following winter and heavy mortality in Iceland. It is a major event in the eVolv2k catalogue and the classic case for high-latitude volcanic forcing.
uncertainty: eruption June 1783 to February 1784

label: Unidentified tropical eruption of 1809
detail: A large ice-core sulfate signal from an unidentified tropical volcano, six years before Tambora. Its lingering cooling complicates attribution of the 1816 anomaly, which is why Tambora anomalies are often computed relative to 1814.
uncertainty: ice-core dated 1808/1809; source unknown

label: Dalton Minimum
detail: A period of low solar activity spanning solar cycles 4 to 7, with somewhat higher sunspot numbers than the Maunder Minimum and sunspots in both hemispheres. It coincided with lower global temperatures, but the causal link is not well established and it is generally not classed as a true grand minimum.
uncertainty: about 1790-1830, given as 1796-1820 in some sources

label: Tambora eruption, Sumbawa
detail: The largest eruption of the instrumental era. Stratospheric sulfate shielded incoming sunlight for about three years. Sulfur isotopes now constrain its plume height in the eVolv2k version 4 catalogue, but large uncertainties remain in the altitude and hemispheric distribution of the aerosol.
uncertainty: climactic eruption 10-11 April 1815

label: The Year Without a Summer
detail: The Northern Hemisphere summer after Tambora brought crop failure and food shortage across Europe and North America, and the coldest European summer between 1766 and 2000. Raible and colleagues give annual cooling of 0.4 to 0.8 C for the tropics and Northern Hemisphere extratropics relative to the preceding 30 years; the widely quoted 0.4 to 0.7 C global-mean figure comes from elsewhere and should not be attributed to that review. The 1809 eruption, the Dalton Minimum and the tail of the Little Ice Age all contribute to the background.
uncertainty: cooling 0.4-0.8 C for the tropics and NH extratropics; no strong Southern Hemisphere signal

label: Instrumental baseline begins
detail: The period 1850 to 1900 is the reference the IPCC and WMO use for pre-industrial, and 1850 is where the long global surface-temperature datasets start. Every modern warming number in this project is anchored here, which is why it belongs on the deep-time chart as the join between proxy and thermometer.
uncertainty: the 1850-1900 mean itself carries observational uncertainty

label: Krakatau eruption
detail: The eruption that produced the largest perturbation to the stratospheric aerosol layer before Pinatubo, with globally observed optical effects and measurable cooling. It is the last major event inside the eVolv2k window, which closes at 1900 CE.
uncertainty: climactic eruption 26-27 August 1883

label: Keeling begins measuring CO2
detail: C. David Keeling of Scripps Institution of Oceanography began continuous direct atmospheric CO2 measurement at Mauna Loa Observatory in March 1958, producing the Keeling Curve. NOAA began its own parallel measurements there in May 1974. This is the moment the CO2 record stops being a proxy and becomes an instrument reading.

label: Hansen's Senate testimony
detail: On 23 June 1988 James Hansen told the US Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that 1988 was the warmest year of the instrumental record, that the warming could be attributed to the greenhouse effect with high confidence, and that models showed the greenhouse effect already changing the odds of extreme events. The companion paper, Hansen and colleagues in the Journal of Geophysical Research, published forecasts under three emissions scenarios running annually to 2019. Contemporaries criticised the stated confidence; the trajectory was substantially right.
uncertainty: the often-quoted 99 percent applied specifically to the warming being a real trend rather than noise

label: Mount Pinatubo eruption
detail: About 17 to 20 Tg of SO2 was injected into the stratosphere, the largest such perturbation since Krakatau. The cloud circled the Earth in three weeks, with peak local mid-visible optical depth of 0.4 in late 1992 and global values of 0.1 to 0.15 for two years. Observed global cooling reached about 0.5 C at the surface and 0.6 C in the troposphere in mid-1992, close to the GISS model forecast made before the cooling happened, which is one of the cleanest successful predictions in climate science.
uncertainty: climactic eruption 15 June 1991; the 0.5 C cooling figure is being reassessed

label: Kyoto Protocol adopted
detail: The first treaty to set binding emissions targets, covering six greenhouse gases with differentiated Annex B targets against a 1990 baseline, for example -8 percent for the EU-15 and -7 percent for the United States, over a first commitment period of 2008 to 2012.
uncertainty: adoption 11 December 1997; the entry-into-force date was not stated on the page we read

label: CO2 passes 400 ppm at Mauna Loa
detail: The monthly mean CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa exceeded 400 ppm for the first time in May 2013. The 800,000-year ice-core record has no comparable value: its interglacial maxima top out near 300 ppm. The crossing is checkable directly against the NOAA monthly-mean file.
uncertainty: monthly means are subject to quality-control revision

label: Paris Agreement adopted
detail: Adopted on 12 December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016, with 194 Parties as of 27 January 2026. It commits Parties to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 C.

label: Warmest year on record, first above 1.5 C
detail: The WMO consolidated analysis of six datasets, from ECMWF, the Japan Meteorological Agency, NASA, NOAA, the Met Office and Berkeley Earth, put 2024 at 1.55 C above the 1850 to 1900 average, the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 C above pre-industrial. The ten years 2015 to 2024 are the ten warmest on record. A single year above 1.5 C is not a breach of the Paris goal, which is assessed as a multi-decadal average.
uncertainty: +/- 0.13 C on the 1.55 C figure

label: CO2 at 429 ppm
detail: The Mauna Loa monthly mean for July 2026, published by NOAA GML on 5 August 2026 and read on 8 August 2026, was 429.12 ppm. That is roughly 150 ppm above the pre-industrial Law Dome value and about 250 ppm above the deepest glacial minimum of 172 ppm in the EPICA record. It is the right-hand end of every chart in this project.
uncertainty: monthly means are subject to quality-control revision
